headline: 15 inches of rain in one day. It's Florida's dry season.
summary: A slow storm sat over Broward County and dropped 15.3 inches of rain in the 24 hours to Wednesday. Hollywood declared an emergency, parts of I-95 and the Turnpike closed under water, and the roof of Temple Sinai fell in. No one was hurt. Schools in Broward and Miami-Dade are closed Thursday. Another 12 inches could fall by Friday.

cover_question.q: Could it rain that much here?

cover_answer: Big storms happen anywhere. This one is parked over Florida.
table_question: A driver's wake pushes water into your home. Whose fault is that?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Florida it rained so hard that cars stopped in the water on the big roads. Fifteen inches fell in one day, about up to your knee. Nobody got hurt, and kids there get Thursday off school while it drains. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Knee-deep is rain they can measure on themselves. The rest is for us.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so 15 inches of rain becomes water up to their own knee. Cantor found the picture frightens this age more than the fact, so 'nobody got hurt' comes right after the stalled cars. Expect 'could it rain that much here?' Big storms happen anywhere. This one is over Florida.

8-12.script: A slow storm parked over Broward County, Florida, and dropped 15.3 inches of rain in a day. Water covered the highway and stalled the cars on it. Drivers who kept going fast pushed waves into people's homes, like someone running through a puddle beside you. Nobody was hurt.
8-12.why: A wave from a car is a chain they have felt in a puddle.
8-12.why_long: At eight a child is working out cause and effect, so the script hands them a chain: a storm parks, 15.3 inches fall, the road floods, a fast car makes a wave, the wave goes into a house. The puddle is a mechanism they know from their own shoes. Expect 'why did the roof fall?' The report says heavy rain, and no more.

13-17.script: Why is it pouring in Florida's dry season? A Weather Service meteorologist blames El Niño, a natural cycle steering storms south. Second: the state warned Tuesday night of 'potentially catastrophic' rain, and Wednesday cars still stalled on I-95. Whose call was it to stay home?
13-17.why: Two things at once: a natural cycle, and a warning that came early.
13-17.why_long: A sixteen-year-old can hold two true things: El Niño is a natural cycle, and the state's warning was out the night before the cars stalled. The script gives them both, then a question with no clean answer. Expect 'is this climate change?' The report blames El Niño and says nothing about climate change. Leave it there.

5-7.q: Could it rain that much here?
5-7.a: Big storms can happen anywhere. Grown-ups know what to do: stay off the roads until the water drains away.

8-12.a: The report says heavy rain caused it, and nothing more. Nobody was hurt.
No. Another 12 inches could fall on Florida's Atlantic coast by Friday.

13-17.a: It is, October to May. The Weather Service blames El Niño this year.
The report says El Niño and doesn't mention climate change. That's all.
